content: Scrub typhus is a significant cause of acute febrile illness in Asia and is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular bacterium. The antibiotics commonly used to treat scrub typhus include tetracyclines, chloramphenicol, macrolides, and rifampicin. The purpose of this review was to evaluate and compare the efficacy of different antibiotic regimens for the treatment of scrub typhus. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was performed up to January 8, 2018. These databases included the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group specialized trials register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and the metaRegister of Controlled Trials (mRCT). References were checked, and study authors were contacted for additional data. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that compared antibiotic regimens in patients diagnosed with scrub typhus based on clinical symptoms and compatible laboratory tests, excluding the Weil-Felix test. Seven trials were included in the review, comprising six RCTs and one quasi-RCT, with a total of 548 participants. These trials were conducted in the Asia-Pacific region, specifically in Korea (three trials), Malaysia (one trial), and Thailand (three trials). Only one trial included children under the age of 15 (57 participants). Five of the trials were judged to have a high risk of performance and detection bias due to inadequate blinding. The trials varied in terms of dosing regimens and outcome measures. Overall, treatment failure rates were low across the studies. Two trials compared doxycycline with tetracycline. The evidence regarding differences in treatment failure between these two antibiotics is highly uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Doxycycline may result in little or no difference in the resolution of fever within 48 hours compared to tetracycline (risk ratio [RR] 1.14, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.90 to 1.44; 55 participants; one trial; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, there may be little or no difference in the time to defervescence (116 participants; one trial; low-certainty evidence). Data for other outcomes could not be extracted. Three trials compared doxycycline with macrolides. For most outcomes, including treatment failure, resolution of fever within 48 hours, time to defervescence, and serious adverse events, the evidence is very uncertain regarding any differences between doxycycline and macrolides (very low-certainty evidence). Macrolides may result in little or no difference in the proportion of patients achieving fever resolution within five days compared to doxycycline (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.10; 185 participants; two trials; low-certainty evidence). One trial compared azithromycin with either doxycycline or chloramphenicol in children. However, it was not possible to separate the data for the doxycycline/chloramphenicol group, limiting the analysis. One trial compared doxycycline with rifampicin. For all outcomes, the evidence is very uncertain regarding any differences between these two antibiotics (very low-certainty evidence). Notably, this trial deviated from its protocol after three out of eight patients receiving a combination of doxycycline and rifampicin experienced treatment failure. Across the trials, mild gastrointestinal side effects were more frequently reported with doxycycline compared to other antibiotics. In conclusion, tetracycline, doxycycline, azithromycin, and rifampicin are effective treatment options for scrub typhus, with few reported treatment failures. Chloramphenicol remains a potential treatment option, but it was not directly compared in this review. Most of the available evidence is of low or very low certainty. Some low-certainty evidence suggests that there may be little or no difference in efficacy between tetracycline, doxycycline, and azithromycin. Given the very low-certainty evidence for rifampicin and the potential risk of inducing resistance in undiagnosed tuberculosis cases, rifampicin should not be considered a first-line treatment option. It may be considered as a second-line treatment after ruling out active tuberculosis. Further research is needed, including adequately powered trials comparing doxycycline with azithromycin or other macrolides, as well as trials investigating other candidate antibiotics such as rifampicin. Studies should also focus on treatments for severe scrub typhus. Standardization of diagnostic methods and clinical outcome reporting is essential to enable robust comparisons across studies.
